newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Arboyne says nears Nonoc decision.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Arboyne says nears Nonoc decision.

text.p: Arboyne NL chief executive Steve Kesler said any decision to reopen the long-dormant Nonoc nickel mine and refinery in the Philippines depended on a feasibility study which was nearing completion.
Kesler, speaking from Manila, denied some media reports which said Pacific Nickel Holdings Ltd had committed 16.65 billion pesos, or about US$650 million, to revive Nonoc.
The intention was that Arboyne would raise the equity to finance rehabilitation of the property, he told Reuters.
It was not correct to say that a decision had been taken to reopen the mine in June of this year. "That is not correct. The feasibility study is still in the course of finalisation," Kesler said.
Pacific Nickel and Arboyne-owned Philnico had been undertaking studies related to recommissioning the mine and refinery. Due diligence work was on-going, he said.

Philnico holds rights to acquire the assets of Nonoc from the Asset Privatisation Trust of the Philippine government. This right was achieved via an option which Arboyne has to acquire Pacific Nickel, which currently has the rights to buy the mine and refinery.
Joint lead managers for the equity raising and financial advisers for the debt arrangement had been appointed, Kesler said.

In late February Arboyne obtained approval to raise an additional A$20 million to initiate early rehabilitation work on the island of Nonoc to ensure fast mobilisation when contracts were awarded, he said.
Asked if it was felt likely that the project would go ahead, Kesler said: "Every project is subject to feasibility studies and due diligence."
The only figure of any significance was the US$500 million-plus cost of fully refurbishing the project which Arboyne had announced to shareholders, he said.
Expected time of construction was about 18 months, he said.

If feasibility studies signal a go-ahead, Arboyne will change its name to Pacific Nickel Ltd, a name it has registered with the Australian Stock Exchange, and exercise its option to acquire Pacific Nickel Holdings.
Pacific Nickel, as full owner of Philnico and the Nonoc asssets, would then undertake a global equity offering.
The Nonoc refinery was originally rated at 31,000 tonnes of nickel and 1,500 tonnes of cobalt a year.
Arboyne was examining ways of de-bottlenecking the plant to increase output, he said.

The project, then known as New York-listed Marinduque Mining and Industrial Corp, was started up in the mid-1970s and operated until 1986, when it was closed as a result of oil price hikes. It was then acquired by the Philippine government's Asset Privatisation Trust and has been up for sale ever since.
